responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response:
Red.

Reason: Pressing red never makes you worse off and can only help.
- If blue is the majority, everyone survives regardless of what you press.
- If red is the majority, only red pressers survive.

So red is a (weakly) dominant choice: you survive whether the world ends up red or blue. If everyone reasons this way, everyone presses red and everyone survives.

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
I press red.

Why
- Holding everyone else’s choices fixed, red never makes you worse off and sometimes makes you better off.
  - If the majority is blue, everyone survives regardless of your choice, so red is as good as blue.
  - If the majority is red, only red pressers survive, so red is strictly better than blue.
- That makes red a weakly dominant strategy for individual survival (maximin/”safety-first” reasoning). Even if your vote could swing the outcome (e.g., others are tied), you survive either way by pressing red.

Notes
- Both “all blue” and “all red” are stable outcomes in which everyone survives. Red is appealing because it guarantees your survival even if others don’t coordinate on blue.

Steelmanning “press blue”
- Superrational/correlated reasoning: In a fully symmetric, anonymous problem where many agents reason like you, your choice is strong evidence of what those agents will do. Choosing blue is choosing the policy you’d want universally adopted; if everyone similar follows it, we get the Pareto-best outcome (everyone survives) without creating a red/blue split.
- Altruistic expected value: Your single vote has a tiny chance of being pivotal, but if it is, pressing blue saves essentially everyone, whereas pressing red would condemn about half. In large populations, “tiny pivot chance × enormous stake” can outweigh the personal risk you take by not pressing the individually safe button.
- Moral norm-setting: Endorsing “press blue” establishes a cooperative convention for this and similar coordination problems. It avoids free-riding (pressing red while hoping others press blue) and helps societies converge on norms that yield the best collective results when everyone follows them.
- Pivotal fairness: In the knife-edge case where your vote alone decides the outcome (others are tied), pressing blue strictly helps more people (it saves everyone) at no cost to your own survival in that case—so a rule like “press blue” dominates on moral grounds exactly when your action matters most.

Bottom line
- If your goal is guaranteed personal survival under any behavior by others, press red.
- If your goal is to maximize total lives saved via cooperative/superrational reasoning and norm-setting, press blue.

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
Short answer: With private choices and no coordination, most people press red. Blue gets a meaningful minority from prosocial, high-trust, and “superrational” cohorts.

Who tends to press red (individual-survival/risk-dominant logic)
- Classical decision theorists and game theorists using dominance or maximin reasoning (CDT/EDT). They see red as weakly dominant.
- Low-trust environments: People from societies or communities with low generalized trust/weak institutions (per World Values Survey “trust” items). When you expect others not to coordinate, red is safer.
- Proself/individualist social value orientation (SVO): People who reliably pick self-favoring options in social dilemmas.
- High risk aversion or strong personal-responsibility heuristics: “Control what you can control” types, survival-focused mindsets, people with heavy dependents who prioritize ensuring their own survival for their family’s sake.
- Cynics/free-riders: Those who hope “enough others press blue so we all live,” but still pick red because it can’t hurt them.
- Norms built around safety-first engineering/operations thinking when there’s no way to verify others (red is the risk-dominant equilibrium).

Who tends to press blue (cooperative/policy-based logic)
- Superrationalists/functional decision theorists (Hofstadter/FDT): People who think “my choice is evidence about what similar reasoners do,” and who adopt the policy that, if widely mirrored, maximizes lives. Many in rationalist/EA-adjacent communities explicitly endorse this.
- Prosocial SVO and high-empathy/agreeableness profiles: People who routinely cooperate in public-goods and prisoner’s-dilemma experiments even at personal risk.
- High-trust cultures and tight, norm-following groups with strong cooperative expectations (e.g., communities with robust public-goods provision and strong compliance norms). If you believe most others will pick blue, blue is both moral and safe.
- Altruistic/mission-driven subcultures: Effective altruists, humanitarian workers, some religious or communal orders that prioritize “do the good action even if others defect,” and people motivated by norm-setting (“model the cooperative rule you want everyone to follow”).
- One-boxers in Newcomb-like problems: People who already accept trading off a sure personal edge to get the globally best outcome via correlated reasoning.

Swing factors that shift people either way
- Public signals and common knowledge: If credible mass messaging convinces people “almost everyone will press blue,” many fence-sitters switch to blue. If messaging is noisy or polarizing, red dominates.
- Visibility and accountability: If choices were public or reputationally tracked, blue would surge; private choice pushes red.
- Group identity coupling: If you think “people like me read the same arguments and will do what I do,” you’re more likely to pick blue; if you feel uncorrelated with others, you pick red.

Bottom line forecast
- Absent credible global coordination and with strictly private action, red wins a clear majority due to risk-dominant reasoning and free-riding. Blue still attracts a noticeable minority clustered in high-trust, prosocial, and superrational niches.

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: No. Pressing blue can be perfectly rational, depending on goals, beliefs, and decision theory. It’s only “irrational” under a narrow, self-only, dominance-based view.

When pressing blue is rational
- You value others’ survival substantially (altruistic utility), not just your own. Your action is pivotal with small probability but affects billions if it is. With N ≈ 8e9 people and a near-50/50 expectation, the chance your vote is exactly pivotal is about √(2/(πN)) ≈ 9×10^-6. In that knife-edge case, pressing blue saves roughly half of humanity more than pressing red. Expected other-lives saved is on the order of 0.4√N ≈ 36,000 lives—often swamping your personal risk if you weight others’ lives meaningfully.
- You use superrational/functional decision theory. In a symmetric, private-choice setup, your policy is strong evidence about what similar reasoners do. Adopting “press blue” helps coordinate that whole correlated cluster toward the Pareto-best outcome (everyone survives) and reduces the risk of a red/blue split.
- You believe most others will press blue (high-trust prior). Then blue is both cooperative and personally safe.
- You follow rule- or virtue-based norms that aim to establish cooperative conventions across problems, not just maximize your own survival in this instance.

When pressing blue is irrational
- Your utility is only your own survival, and you treat others’ choices as independent of yours. Then red weakly dominates: if blue wins you live either way; if red wins you only live if you pressed red.
- You assign overwhelming probability that the majority will be red no matter what, and you don’t weight others’ survival enough to offset the personal risk.
- You are extremely risk-averse about your own life relative to any benefit to others.

Bottom line
- Under classical, self-only dominance reasoning, blue is irrational.
- Under altruistic, superrational, or norm-setting reasoning—and even under standard expected-value calculations with meaningful weight on others’ lives—pressing blue is a rational choice.
